cards.canonical_statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, f(x)=y is solvable exactly when every linear functional on W annihilating all outputs of f also annihilates y.
cards.proof_strategy: A solution makes every annihilating functional vanish on y by direct substitution.
sketch_steps: A solution makes every annihilating functional vanish on y by direct substitution.
Conversely these tests put y in the double annihilator of range f.
A subspace over a field equals its double annihilator; the separation argument uses the quotient by that subspace.
Membership in the range supplies the desired solution, giving the finite-dimensional Fredholm alternative.

cards.canonical_statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, if a nonzero u lies in ker f, then for every x the distinct vector x+u has the same image as x. Thus any soluble right-hand side is nonunique.
cards.proof_strategy: Choose an arbitrary solution vector x.
sketch_steps: Choose an arbitrary solution vector x.
Adding a kernel vector leaves its image unchanged by linearity.
If x+u=x, additive cancellation would force u=0.
The assumed nonzero kernel vector therefore constructs a distinct solution for every soluble right-hand side.

cards.canonical_statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, if A B=I on Kⁿ for rectangular A:n×m and B:m×n, then Bx=By forces x=y; a left inverse certifies uniqueness of input coordinates.
cards.proof_strategy: Start from an equality of two outputs of B.
sketch_steps: Start from an equality of two outputs of B.
Apply the known left inverse A to that equality.
Associativity combines the two matrix actions as AB.
The identity action recovers equality of the input vectors.

cards.proof_strategy: Expand the product of I−N with the finite geometric sum.

Successive powers cancel telescopically, leaving I−N^k.

The same telescoping in reverse multiplication order proves both inverse identities, including the degenerate k=0 case under its premise.

cards.canonical_statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, if neither S⊆T nor T⊆S, there are u∈S and y∈T whose sum belongs to neither S nor T; their union fails closure under addition.
cards.proof_strategy: Choose u in S but outside T, and y in T but outside S.
sketch_steps: Choose u in S but outside T, and y in T but outside S.
If u+y lay in S, subtracting u would put y in S, a contradiction.
If u+y lay in T, subtracting y would put u in T, also a contradiction.
Both summands lie in the union but their sum does not.

cards.canonical_statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, a vector in the span of a finite family has coefficients giving it as a finite linear combination, and conversely.
cards.proof_strategy: The coefficient-to-vector map sends a to its finite combination.
sketch_steps: The coefficient-to-vector map sends a to its finite combination.
Its range is the span of the family.
A span member therefore has a preimage coefficient function.
Conversely every such finite combination lies in the span.

cards.proof_strategy: Select the two equal vectors at different indices.
sketch_steps: Select the two equal vectors at different indices.
Independence over a field makes the family indexing function injective.
Their equality would force the two indices to coincide.
This contradicts distinctness and detects the repeated-vector dependence.

cards.canonical_statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, if span(v) meets ker f only at zero, the image family f(vᵢ) is linearly independent exactly when v is; global injectivity of f is unnecessary.
cards.proof_strategy: A relation among image vectors is the image of a relation among the original vectors.
sketch_steps: A relation among image vectors is the image of a relation among the original vectors.
The latter sum lies both in span(v) and in ker f.
Their trivial intersection forces that sum to be zero, so original independence kills its coefficients.
For the converse any original zero relation maps to an image relation; no control of f away from span(v) is needed.

cards.proof_strategy: A basis provides both independent vectors and a spanning family.

cards.canonical_statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, replacing any one vector of a basis by zero produces a same-length family whose span omits the replaced vector; having the right number of vectors is not sufficient for a basis.
cards.proof_strategy: Use the ith coordinate functional of the original basis.
sketch_steps: Use the ith coordinate functional of the original basis.
It annihilates every vector in the modified family: the ith is zero, all other basis vectors have ith coordinate zero.
Therefore it annihilates the whole modified span.
Its value on the removed basis vector is one, so that vector cannot belong to the new span.

cards.proof_strategy: Every linear map sends the zero vector to zero.
sketch_steps: Every linear map sends the zero vector to zero.
A translation sends zero to its translation vector u.
Agreement with a linear map would force u=0.
The nonzero hypothesis therefore gives a general family of nonlinear affine maps.

cards.canonical_statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, an idempotent linear map splits the whole space as the direct sum of its range and kernel.
sketch_steps: For every x, write x=f(x)+(x−f(x)).
The first summand lies in the range, and idempotency puts the second in the kernel.
A vector in both the range and the kernel is fixed by f and also sent to zero, hence is zero.
These spanning and trivial-intersection statements give the direct-sum decomposition.

cards.proof_strategy: Form the block matrix with identity diagonal blocks and off-diagonal A and B.

Eliminating one block or the other gives the rectangular Sylvester determinant identity.

The equal determinants transfer solvability and uniqueness for all right-hand sides between the two different-sized systems.
